implementation_notes: The C++20 ranges library provides the pattern's two halves: a view is a lightweight, non-owning range that computes its elements on demand, and range adaptors are composable objects (views::filter, views::transform, views::take, views::join, views::chunk, ...) that chain with operator| into a pipeline applied lazily while it is iterated. The adaptor-closure form lets a pipeline be stored and reused (auto pipeline = views::filter(pred) | views::transform(f); then anyRange | pipeline), and any range is a source while any range algorithm, range-for or range conversion (std::ranges::to, C++23) is a sink. What replaces the classic structure: there is no accumulator or reduction protocol inside the value at all - the compiler instantiates the nested view types and usually inlines them into one loop, so the reducing-function transformer is unnecessary. The classic transducer is justified only when the pipeline must also drive a non-range sink (a channel, an event loop, a batch writer) or must be erased behind a single named type.
pitfalls: A view does not own its base: composing over a temporary or a local that dies (auto v = make_vector() | vw::transform(f)) leaves a dangling view - keep the owner alive or materialise.

Views are re-evaluated per traversal: iterating the same pipeline twice recomputes filter and transform, and a view over an input range is also single-pass - materialise (std::ranges::to) when the result is used more than once.
The pipeline type is unnameable and grows with each adaptor; keep it as auto or inside a lambda instead of writing the type out, and prefer views::all_t where a named type is required.

variants.name: range-v3 views (C++14/17)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++20, range-v3 is the working realisation of the same idea - its manual states that the code is the basis of the C++20 range support - so the same 'transformations composed as values' pipeline is available on C++14/17 toolchains: header-only views and adaptor closures with the operator| syntax, eager composable actions for in-place container work, and view_facade for hand-written lazy sources. Choose it when the toolchain is below C++20 or when a view outside the standard set (zip, group_by, sliding, chunk) is needed. What replaces the classic structure: exactly as with std::views, the composition is the pipeline and the accumulator is supplied by whatever consumes it; the cost of the replacement is a third-party dependency and the same non-owning lifetime rules.
pitfalls: The adaptors are non-owning exactly like std::views: they hold references into the source range, so the source must outlive the pipeline.

The range-v3 manual warns the library evolves without regard for backwards compatibility (only the ranges::cpp20 namespace is frozen); pin the version and do not mix range-v3 views into a std::ranges pipeline or vice versa.
Deep pipelines produce deeply nested view types: compile times and error messages explode, so split long chains into named intermediate stages.

variants.name: hand-written reducing-function transformer (C++11)
variants.idiom_name: hand-written reducing-function transformer: rf -> rf, composed with ordinary function composition
variants.implementation_notes: The literal pattern in C++: a transducer is a template that takes a reducing function and returns a wrapped reducing function, so stages are ordinary function objects composed with each other and the sink supplies the accumulation ('the job'). This is the form to choose when the pipeline must drive a destination that is not a range - an io_uring completion, a channel, a batch executor - or when the whole pipeline must be stored as one erased type (std::function, std::function_ref) and paid for once. What the ranges variants do better: no accumulator plumbing and no arity protocol, and the compiler can still inline everything; the transducer form re-invents the completion and early-termination protocol (an init call, a completion call, a stop flag) that ranges simply do not need.
pitfalls: Stateful stages (take, dedupe, partition) need per-application state; capturing it in the lambda turns the transducer into a one-shot value that corrupts results when applied twice or from two threads.
The protocol must carry its own early-termination signal and completion call, or take/drop stages keep consuming the source and buffering stages lose their tail.
Each stage is a lambda-to-lambda call per element; behind std::function or without inlining the composed pipeline can be slower than the hand-written loop it replaced.
